newsitem.title: USA: Clinton angry Democrats stopped scanning donations.
newsitem.headline: Clinton angry Democrats stopped scanning donations.

text.p: President Clinton Monday said he felt "sick at heart" when he first learned his Democratic Party accepted illegal political contributions from foreign sources and was angry that donations were not checked more carefully.
In an interview with Fox News Channel, Clinton said he was confident that more careful scrutiny of the political contributions would have exposed the illegal contributions before they were accepted.

"The first time I found that the Democratic Party had taken any money that was not from American citizens, I was sick at heart and I was angry that the checking hadn't been in," Clinton said. "It's clear to me that if the proper procedures had been in place, they would have found it out."
He said he was also angry because the fund-raising controversy gave the Democrats an "unfair image" although the funds in question represented less than 2 percent of the money raised in 1996.
"What about the other million plus people that helped that were perfectly legal. What about the other 98-1/2 percent of the money that was raised that was perfectly legal," he said.

A Senate committee has completed four weeks of hearings into campaign finance irregularities, exposing some sleazy aspects of Clinton's 1996 re-election campaign, but thus far no hard evidence of any sinister foreign plots against America.

Republicans began the hearings by suggesting that espionage was involved in campaign finance scandals or that the Chinese government tried to influence the outcome of the 1996 presidential election, but those allegations have not been proven thus far.

In the interview, Clinton said the revelations about illegal and improper fund-raising by both parties in 1996 underscored the need for Congress to approve legislation reforming campaign finance laws.

He reiterated his call for curbs on unlimited political contributions to the parties, and said broadcasters should offer candidates free air time in exchange for the digital space on the airwaves they got for free from the government.
